subject: Cost segregation changes timing — model the trade-offs
preheader: No universal price cutoff or payback · loss limits, recapture, and hold period matter

marketSnapshot.headline: Cost segregation — a timing analysis, not a promised saving
marketSnapshot.body: A defensible cost-segregation study may classify eligible components into shorter recovery periods than the residential building. The result is property- and taxpayer-specific. Basis, acquisition and placed-in-service dates, bonus-depreciation eligibility, passive-activity and other loss limits, study cost, recapture, and sale timing all affect the after-tax present value. Review current IRS Publication 946 and the IRS Cost Segregation Audit Technique Guide with a qualified tax professional.

dealSpotter.body: Build two adviser-reviewed scenarios using the property's supported basis allocation: the regular depreciation schedule and the proposed study classifications. Apply the taxpayer's actual loss limitations, acquisition and placed-in-service dates, study fee, discount rate, expected sale or exchange, and recapture treatment. A larger deduction on paper does not prove a current cash-tax benefit.

dealSpotter.headlineNumber: Study cost is only one input
dealSpotter.body: There is no responsible universal purchase-price or gross-rent cutoff. A lower depreciable basis may make a study harder to justify, but fee quotes, component mix, available losses, expected hold, and recapture matter. Ask for a written feasibility estimate and compare it with a no-study scenario before commissioning the work.

dealSpotter.headlineNumber: Exit timing can change the result
dealSpotter.body: A near-term taxable sale can reduce or reverse the value of accelerating deductions once study cost, depreciation-related gain treatment, suspended losses, and time value are included. A section 1031 exchange may postpone recognition only if all requirements are met; it does not automatically eliminate recapture or make the original study worthwhile.

blogFeature.title: 1031 exchange basics: how to defer capital gains on rental property
blogFeature.excerpt: Cost segregation changes depreciation timing; a qualifying section 1031 exchange may postpone recognition of gain. Neither step guarantees tax savings or a higher IRR, and both require property- and taxpayer-specific review.

qa.question: Should I do cost seg on every rental I buy?
qa.answer: No universal rule makes cost segregation a clear win. Ask a qualified tax professional to model the supported component classification, study fee, bonus-depreciation eligibility, passive-activity and other loss limits, basis and at-risk limits, expected hold, taxable-sale or exchange scenario, recapture, and time value. Real-estate-professional status does not by itself make every rental loss usable; material participation and other limits still apply. Commission a study only after the property-specific comparison supports it.
